growth_011:n1.prompt:
You are helping me run keyword and topic research for our SEO & content engine's first stage. Before starting, ask me for: (1) our domain/site URL, (2) our product/service description and target customer, (3) 3-5 competitor domains if I have them, and (4) any existing keyword or content list we've already used, so you avoid duplicates.

Goal: produce a prioritized list of 15-25 keyword/topic candidates for our next content batch.

Actions to take:
1. Use Google Search (and Google Autocomplete/'People also ask' style queries) to explore terms related to our product and audience, noting search intent (informational, commercial, navigational) for each.
2. Check what content currently ranks for promising terms by searching them directly and noting the top-ranking pages, their format (blog, listicle, comparison, tool page), and approximate depth.
3. If competitor domains are provided, look at their visible blog/resource sections (via site search like 'site:competitor.com blog' or browsing their sitemap page if public) to spot topics they cover that we don't.
4. Group candidate keywords into topic clusters (e.g. by theme or funnel stage) and estimate relative competitiveness qualitatively (low/medium/high) based on the type and authority of ranking pages you observed — do not fabricate exact search volume or difficulty numbers you cannot verify.
5. For each keyword, write a one-line note on suggested content angle and target intent.

Done looks like: a single organized list (table or grouped bullets) of keyword candidates with cluster/theme, intent, qualitative competitiveness, and a suggested angle — ready to hand to a writer or drafting agent next.

Report back with: the full prioritized keyword list, the clusters/themes identified, any notable competitor gaps found, and flag any keywords where you were uncertain about intent or competitiveness so I can review before we move to drafting.

growth_011:n2.prompt:
You are helping me run the drafting stage of my SEO content loop. Before starting, ask me for anything you don't already have: (1) my domain and a short description of my business/product, (2) the target keyword or keyword cluster for this piece (from our keyword research step), (3) the search intent and target audience, (4) desired content type (blog post, landing page, guide, comparison, etc.), (5) target word count, (6) tone/style guidance or example posts to match voice, and (7) any internal pages or resources I want linked.

Once you have these, draft a complete piece of content:
- A compelling, SEO-aware title (under ~60 characters) and a meta description (under ~155 characters).
- A logical heading structure (H1/H2/H3) that covers the topic thoroughly and matches search intent.
- Body copy in clean Markdown, written for humans first, naturally incorporating the target keyword and related terms without stuffing.
- Suggested internal links (using the pages I gave you) and, where useful, placeholders for external citations or data.
- A short list of 3-5 alt-text suggestions if images would help.

Do not publish anything or touch the live site — this draft is for human review and editing next in the loop. When done, output the full draft in Markdown in your response (or save it to a clearly named file if I've given you file access) and give me a one-paragraph summary covering: the keyword targeted, word count achieved, and any gaps or assumptions you made that I should double-check during editing. Ask me if you need clarification on intent or scope before drafting.

growth_011:n3.prompt:
You are helping me prepare an AI-drafted article for editorial review before publication. If you don't already have them, ask me for: (1) the draft content or a link/file path to it, (2) our brand voice/style guide or examples of past published posts, (3) the target keyword and content brief this draft was written against, and (4) which CMS or platform we publish to (so you know the review workflow context).

Once you have these, please:
1. Read the draft closely and compare it against our style guide and past posts, flagging any tone, voice, or formatting inconsistencies.
2. Check factual claims, statistics, quotes, and any cited sources for accuracy or unsupported assertions — flag anything that looks wrong, outdated, or unverifiable.
3. Check that the draft actually addresses the target keyword and content brief (coverage, structure, headings, internal linking opportunities).
4. Identify weak transitions, redundant sections, unclear explanations, or SEO issues (missing title tag/meta description, thin sections, missing alt text placeholders).
5. Produce a consolidated editorial memo: a bullet list of issues found (categorized as voice, accuracy, structure, SEO), each with the specific location in the draft and a suggested fix or rewritten passage.
6. If the CMS supports draft comments or suggested edits, prepare those as inline suggestions rather than applying them directly, so a human editor can accept or reject each one.

Do not mark the article as approved, do not publish it, and do not change its status in the CMS. This step requires a human editor to make the final accept/reject call on content quality, voice, and accuracy. Please compile your findings into a clear editorial review memo and then stop for human sign-off, presenting the memo and suggested edits for my review.

growth_011:n4.prompt:
You are helping me complete the 'Publish to the site' step of our SEO content loop. Our published content lives in a git repo (or a local folder of built site files) that deploys through {{vendor}}, our edge-platform hosting provider. If you don't already know it, ask me for: (1) the repo path or local folder containing the finished, human-edited article/site build, (2) my {{vendor}} site/project identifier, and (3) whether I want a CLI-based deploy or an API-based deploy triggered from your side using my configured credentstials.

Once you have these, do the following:
1. Confirm the content build is up to date (run the site's build command if one exists) and that the new article file(s) are included.
2. Deploy the built site to production using {{vendor}}'s deployment mechanism — either by running its CLI production deploy command, or by calling its documented deploy API endpoint for the given site ID, using my configured credentials. Do not use manual dashboard steps if a CLI/API path is available.
3. If the project is git-connected, verify that pushing to the tracked branch is enough to trigger an automatic deploy, and confirm the deploy fired rather than triggering it redundantly.
4. Poll or check the deploy status until it reports live/success, and fetch the resulting live URL.
5. Verify the new article is reachable at its live URL and renders correctly (title, headings, no broken build).

Done looks like: the new content is live on the production domain, confirmed reachable, with a successful deploy status from {{vendor}}.

Report back: the live URL of the published article, the deploy ID/timestamp, the deploy method used (CLI or API), and any build or deploy warnings encountered.

growth_011:n5.prompt:
You are helping me submit my website's sitemap to search engines as part of our SEO content loop. 

First, ask me for: (1) my domain name, (2) the full URL of my sitemap (typically something like https://yourdomain.com/sitemap.xml — confirm the exact path with me), and (3) whether I already have accounts set up in Google Search Console and Bing Webmaster Tools.

Once you have this info:
1. If I don't have accounts yet, walk me through what's needed to verify domain ownership in Google Search Console and Bing Webmaster Tools (e.g., DNS TXT record, HTML file upload, or meta tag), and prepare the exact values I'd need to add using your configured credentials or dashboard access where possible.
2. If accounts exist and are verified, go into Google Search Console's Sitemaps section and submit the sitemap URL. Do the same in Bing Webmaster Tools' Sitemaps section.
3. Confirm the submission was accepted (not just queued) by checking the status shown in each tool — look for "Success" or "Pending" states and report which one you see.
4. If either tool reports errors (e.g., sitemap not found, invalid format), capture the exact error message and flag it to me rather than attempting to fix the sitemap file itself.

Done looks like: the sitemap URL is successfully submitted in both Google Search Console and Bing Webmaster Tools, with a visible status confirming receipt, OR you've clearly documented what's blocking submission (missing verification, malformed sitemap, etc.).

Report back with: the sitemap URL submitted, the status in each tool, the date/time of submission, and any errors or next steps needed on my end. Do not attempt to modify DNS records, generate new sitemap files, or make site changes — only handle the submission and verification confirmation steps.

growth_011:n6.prompt:
You are helping me monitor content-engine performance in {{vendor}}, our product-analytics tool, as the ongoing final step of our SEO content loop. Goal: build a repeatable view of traffic and ranking signals for published articles so I can see what's working without manual digging.

First, ask me for anything you need: my site domain, which {{vendor}} workspace/project to use, the date range to analyze (default last 30 days), and a list of recently published article URLs or slugs if I have one.

Then, using your configured credentials:
1. Connect to {{vendor}} via its API or MCP server.
2. Confirm pageviews and key interactions (clicks, form submissions, outbound link clicks) are already being captured for our blog/content pages without needing custom tracking code; note any gaps.
3. Run or create queries/dashboards that show: traffic trends per article over time, top-performing pages by visits, referral/search traffic sources, and a funnel or drop-off view from article view to any conversion goal we track (e.g., signup, demo request).
4. If supported, save this as a persistent dashboard or saved insight so it can be revisited without rebuilding.
5. Pull the current numbers and summarize: which articles are gaining traffic, which are flat or declining, and where visitors drop off, in plain language a founder can act on.

Done looks like: a saved dashboard/insight in {{vendor}} covering traffic and drop-off for our content, plus a written summary of top movers and any tracking gaps found.

Report back with: the dashboard link or name, a short summary of findings (top 3 gaining, top 3 declining, key drop-off point if any), and any tracking issues you discovered that need fixing.
